title: Qur'an, Hadith and Sources of Authority
welcome_lead: Approach the sacred texts of Islam — the recited Word of God and the example of the Prophet.
meta_desc: IBDP Religious Studies Adventure: Qur'an, Hadith, Sunnah and Islamic sources of authority.
final_note: You have approached scriptural sources with respect. Their study is central to Islamic life and scholarship.

concepts.def: The recited Word of God revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril (Gabriel) from 610-632 CE.
Way and example of the Prophet Muhammad, preserved especially in the Hadith.
Recorded sayings, actions and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad, classified by reliability.
Major Sunni Hadith collection compiled by al-Bukhari (d. 870).
Qur'anic exegesis, the scholarly tradition of interpreting the Qur'an.
Islamic religious law derived from Qur'an, Sunnah, consensus (ijma) and analogy (qiyas).

walkthroughs.body_html: Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad over 23 years, from his call in 610 CE until his death in 632. It consists of 114 chapters (surahs), arranged broadly from longest to shortest. The Uthmanic codex standardised the text in the mid-7th century.

The Sunnah is preserved in Hadith collections. Sunni Muslims regard six major Sunni collections as most authoritative, especially Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. Each Hadith has a chain of transmitters (isnad) and content (matn); critical study evaluates reliability.

Classical Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh) draws on Qur'an, Sunnah, consensus (ijma) and analogy (qiyas). Sunni schools include Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali. Shia jurisprudence (Ja'fari, etc.) emphasises the role of imams and reasoning (aql). Sharia regulates worship, family life, finance and ethics.
